extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, anatomists, students of biology, and the educated public interested in comparative anatomy and evolution
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and methodological criteria for assessing hypotheses about the origin of species and comparative anatomical claims (especially concerning human vs. ape cerebral structure). Emphasises observational care, multiple lines of evidence, provisional acceptance of hypotheses, and honest scientific practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for a true physical cause (consistency rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A true physical cause is admitted to be such only on one condition -- that it shall account for all the phenomena which come within the range of its operation. If it is inconsistent with any one phenomenon, it must be rejected; if it fails to explain any one phenomenon, it is so far weak, so far to be suspected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a strict test of explanatory hypotheses: check whether the hypothesis can account for all relevant phenomena in its domain. Treat any inconsistency as grounds for rejection or for regarding the hypothesis as provisional. (Huxley applies this standard to Darwin's hypothesis.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional acceptance until missing links are evidenced
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of a hypothesis should be provisional so long as one link in the chain of evidence is wanting; e.g., Darwin's hypothesis is adopted 'subject to the production of proof that physiological species may be produced by selective breeding.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt powerful explanatory hypotheses provisionally when they have high prima facie probability and unify diverse facts, but require the missing empirical links (specific tests/experiments) before full acceptance. Analogous to accepting undulatory theory subject to ether or atomic theory subject to proof of atoms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple independent lines of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If Darwin's hypothesis is admitted, the facts of Development, of Comparative Anatomy, of Geographical Distribution, and of Palaeontology become connected together and exhibit a meaning such as they never possessed before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate hypotheses by how well they integrate independent datasets (developmental, anatomical, biogeographical, palaeontological). Preference for hypotheses that make disparate facts coherent rather than isolated explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational care and appropriate methods (casts, sections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Care is required in observation: the brain loses shape when removed from the skull; a cast of the interior of the skull reproduces general brain form; examine skull sections and make casts to verify natural relations of parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on distorted or extracted specimens. Use appropriate preparatory/replication techniques (plaster casts, skull sections) to determine natural anatomical relations. Beware errors from careless observation or misinterpreting distorted specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-check original sources and specimens; do not suppress contrary facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be compared with earlier figures and statements (e.g., Tiedemann, Schroeder van der Kolk, Vrolik, Gratiolet); unjustified suppression or oversight of prior facts is a serious fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting a novel or controversial anatomical claim, survey and acknowledge previous literature and specimens. Reproduce, compare figures, and investigate discrepancies rather than ignoring or withholding contrary evidence (criticism directed at Professor Owen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid advocacy that smooths over difficulties; be guided by evidence not persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: The author refuses to be an advocate whose business it is to smooth over real difficulties, and insists acceptance should rest on evidence rather than on persuasion where one cannot convince.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars should not downplay problems to promote a favored theory. Transparent exposition of difficulties and limits of current evidence is required; do not mislead public or colleagues by rhetorical smoothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-exaggerate or understate comparative differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Guard against misrepresentation and garbled phraseology that make it seem one says differences are small and insignificant; avoid both denial of a chasm and exaggeration of its magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use balanced, precise language when characterising differences between taxa. Recognise existence and significance of gaps while avoiding hyperbole that misleads about their size or implications for classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification should be based on multiple anatomical characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic distinctions (e.g., placing Man in a separate family) rest chiefly on multiple characters such as dentition, pelvis, and lower limbs; retain the Linnaean order PRIMATES and divide into families of roughly equal systematic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base major taxonomic decisions on a single alleged peculiar structure; weigh a suite of consistent morphological characters. Follow systematic principles (Linnaean framework) and comparable criteria across groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection explains structural differences but must account for reproductive isolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin has satisfactorily proved that selection must occur and can produce forms as distinct structurally as some genera; but selective breeding has yet to be shown to produce physiological species (fertility/sterility issues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating selection as a causal mechanism, require evidence not only of morphological divergence under selection but also demonstration that such processes can yield the reproductive (physiological) separations observed among natural species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of relying on absolute measures without context (brain mass example)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a striking difference in absolute mass between lowest human brain and highest ape, but this has little systematic value because within-human variation can exceed human-ape differences; consider relative and within-group variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret absolute quantitative differences (size, weight) cautiously; assess their systematic significance relative to intraspecific variation and functional/contextual factors rather than treating raw magnitude as decisive.
